subject: EFA and CFA for likert scaled data

messages.author: b38f344d5cde2da0
messages.subject: EFA and CFA for likert scaled data
parts:
Hello, good evening. I'm a master student trying to conduct SEM in my research.
May I ask for your kind suggestions concerning with the 5-point likert scaled data to apply EFA and CFA in R.

My model is
"Safety=~IM1+IM2+IM3+IM4+IM5+IM6+DS1+DS2+DS3+DS4+DS5+DS6+DS7+DS8+DS9
Efficiency=~IM7+IM8+IM9+IM10+IM11+IM12+IM13+DS10+DS11"
The observed variables; IM1 through IM12 & DS1 through DS11 (all variables) are in 5-point likert scaled type from questionnaire survey.

From readings and tests till now, I'm afraid ML does not give the perfect fit instead the serious skewness or kurtosis.
I'd like to request for kind ideas to fit the model.
Thanks a lot for giving time.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: EFA and CFA for likert scaled data
parts:
The observed variables; IM1 through IM12 & DS1 through DS11 (all variables) are in 5-point likert scaled ... serious skewness or kurtosis.

Then it sounds like you should treat them as ordinal:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Hopefully you have several hundred observations.  The asymptotic properties for DWLS estimation of item factor analysis models don't seem to kick in until around N=500.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3162326/

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear Eaindray,

I too have that question… So, I generated data for a population model with the 0.5,0.6,0.7 loadings. Then, I cut the data to make it ordered (5,7 and 9) categories. Then, I random sampled the population with diferente sample sizes (from 30 to 500) and run a CFA on the samples…

 

If your population data is biased, then there are no good estimators since all of them assume that the population is normative…

 

It gets even worse if your population is normative, but by some bias on responses, your sample is completely biased… This happens sometimes:

 

 

The result is not good:

 

 

Cheers,

Jº

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: EFA and CFA for likert scaled data
parts:
Eaindray,
  For the purposes of a Masters thesis, I do not see any harm in trying out some analyses to see what happens with the understanding that any results need to be interpreted in the context of violated assumptions or insufficient sample sizes.  It is still a useful exercise for your professional development and potentially a useful pilot study for your advisor.  (Economists apparently still find it useful to fit linear probability models despite violating OLS assumptions.)

  One strategy might be to propose EFA as the primary analysis and one or more CFA analyses as try-and-see auxiliary analyses.  It might be interesting to write about how consistent the substantive conclusions are across analyses despite the limitations of each.

  Herb Marsh did some research, in the late 1990's I think, that suggested that to some extent having more indicators could compensate for a smaller sample in the context of ML estimation.  You have a fair number of indicators.  So, it may be worth digging up that work.  If I recall correctly, he had a chapter in a book edited by Rick Hoyle on strategies for small sample research which I believe was published by Sage.

  If you are primarily interested in conducting EFA and CFA to extract item statistics for item analysis, you might also compare them to classical item analysis statistics (see the rela and psych packages in R).  There is no gold standard here, but it might be informative to use scatterplots of items to compare various pairs of item statistics.

  Are these new scales or established scales?  New scales with so many items are unlikely to fit a CFA on the first go around.  So, even if you tried that first, you might end up falling back on EFA to figure out what was happening with the items.

  Is your assessment of skewness and kurtosis based on quantitative criteria or based on visual inspection of bar charts?  Sometimes the latter can be misleading.  ML with robust standard errors might be worth trying even if the bar charts look truncated.

  When you write about your study, I would suggest avoiding the use of the term 'bias' to refer to a non-normal univariate distribution.  Even in the context in which it is applied to data, 'bias' has other more common meanings, such as various forms of unrepresentative samples.  Using it to mean non-normality might invite misinterpretation of what you are trying to say.

Good luck,
Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
